function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL and retrieves data as specified by the parameters. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to which the GET request is sent. It is expected to be a well-formed HTTP or HTTPS URL.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: The Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

headers.description: A dictionary of HTTP headers to send with the request. Each key-value pair represents a header name and its value.

timeout.description: The number of seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up, as a float, or a (connect_timeout, read_timeout) tuple. This is a float type value.

lat.description: Latitude of the location for the query, in degrees. This is a float type value.

lon.description: Longitude of the location for the query, in degrees. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters to append to the URL for the GET request.

allow_redirects.description: Determines if HTTP redirections (301, 302, etc.) should be followed.

auth.description: A tuple representing the user credentials for HTTP authentication, typically in the form of (username, password).

cert.description: Path to an SSL certificate file to verify the peer, or a tuple of (certificate file, key file).

cookies.description: A dictionary of cookies to send with the request. The key is the cookie name and the value is the cookie value.

http.description: URL of the proxy for HTTP requests.

https.description: URL of the proxy for HTTPS requests.

proxies.description: A dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy.

stream.description: If True, the response content will not be downloaded immediately but streamed.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not, or a path to a CA bundle if verification is needed.

message.content:
When you’re storing currency valuations (exchange rates, price indices, etc.) that change over time, you want a structure that 1. **Keeps the data ordered by time** – so you can quickly find the rate for a particular date or the most recent rate. 2. **Allows efficient range queries** – e.g., “average rate from Jan 1 2023 to Mar 31 2023”. 3. **Handles sparse updates** – most currencies only change a few times per day, so you don’t want to store a full daily snapshot for every day. 4. **Supports fast inserts/updates** – new rates arrive continuously. A **time‑series‑specific data structure** is usually the best fit. Below are the most common options, ranked by typical use‑case: | # | Data Structure | When to Use | Pros | Cons | |---|----------------|-------------|------|------| | 1 | **Ordered Map / Balanced BST** (e.g., `std::map` in C++, `TreeMap` in Java, `SortedDict` in Python) | Small to medium datasets, single‑process apps | • O(log n) insert, delete, and lookup
• Keeps keys sorted automatically | • Memory overhead per node
• Not ideal for very large series (millions of points) | | 2 | **Segment Tree / Interval Tree** | Need fast range queries (min/max/avg over a period) | • O(log n) query and update
• Can store aggregates (sum, min, max) | • More complex to implement
• Still O(log n) per operation | | 3 | **B‑Tree / B+Tree** (e.g., SQLite, LevelDB, RocksDB) | Persisted storage, large datasets, multi‑process access | • Disk‑friendly, supports millions of rows
• Indexes on timestamp for fast range scans | • Requires a database engine or key‑value store
• Overkill if you only need in‑memory | | 4 | **Time‑Series Database (TSDB)** (InfluxDB, TimescaleDB, Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics) | Production systems, high write throughput, retention policies | • Built‑in compression, down‑sampling, retention
• Query language (SQL/Flux) for aggregates | • Adds infrastructure complexity
• Might be overkill for simple apps | | 5 | **Array of Timestamps + Parallel Array of Values** (e.g., two `std::vector`s) | Very small series, deterministic access pattern | • Minimal overhead, cache‑friendly | • Linear search for arbitrary timestamps unless binary search is used
• No built‑in range aggregation | ### Recommendation for Most Use Cases **Use an ordered map (balanced BST) for in‑memory, single‑process applications**. - Store the key as a timestamp (e.g., `int64_t` epoch seconds or a `DateTime` object). - Store the value as the exchange rate (float/double). ```cpp std::map rates; ``` or in Python: ```python from sortedcontainers import SortedDict rates = SortedDict() # key: datetime, value: float ``` This gives you: - **O(log n)** insertion and lookup. - Easy to get the most recent rate: `rates.peekitem(-1)` (Python) or `rates.rbegin()` (C++). - Range queries via iterators: `auto it = rates.lower_bound(start); while(it != rates.upper_bound(end)) { ... }`. If you anticipate **millions of points** or need **persistent storage**, switch to a **B‑Tree‑based key‑value store** (e.g., RocksDB) or a **TSDB**. Those systems handle compression, retention, and high‑write workloads out of the box. ### Quick‑Start Example (Python) ```python from sortedcontainers import SortedDict from datetime import datetime rates = SortedDict() # Insert a new rate rates[datetime(2023, 1, 1, 12, 0)] = 1.2345 # Lookup exact timestamp rate = rates.get(datetime(2023, 1, 1, 12, 0)) # Get most recent rate most_recent = rates.peekitem(-1)[1] # Range query: average rate between two dates start, end = datetime(2023, 1, 1), datetime(2023, 1, 31) subset = rates.irange(start, end, inclusive=(True, True)) avg_rate = sum(rates[t] for t in subset) / len(subset) ``` ### Bottom Line - **In‑memory, small‑to‑medium** → Ordered map (balanced BST). - **Large, persisted, multi‑process** → B‑Tree or TSDB. Pick the one that matches your scale and persistence needs.
